The house had stood at the end of the lane for more than a century, and nobody in the village could remember a year when it had looked any different. Its walls were covered with ivy so thick that the brickwork showed only in small patches near the ground, and the roof sagged in the middle as if the whole building were slowly exhaling. Children walked past it on their way to school and invented stories about the people who lived inside: a retired sailor, a widow with a parrot, a family that had moved away and simply forgotten to sell. The truth was duller. An old woman named Marta had owned the place since the war, and for the last twenty years she had kept to herself, paying her bills on the first of each month and ordering groceries from the shop by telephone.

Then, one autumn, a van appeared in the drive and three men began carrying boxes into the front room. Marta had fallen in the spring and had gone to live with her sister in another county, and the house was to be sold. The estate agent arrived on a Tuesday with a clipboard and a camera, and spent an hour walking from room to room, writing notes that nobody would read. The floors creaked under her shoes. The kitchen smelled of soap and old paper. In the hall, the light from the stairwell fell in a long dusty column, and she stood in it for a while, listening to the silence, before she remembered to take a photograph.

The neighbours watched from behind their curtains. They had expected a crowd, perhaps an auction, but the sale was quiet and quick. A young couple bought the house in November and moved in before the new year, and for a few weeks the street was full of the sound of hammers and saws. The shutters were taken down and repaired. The ivy was cut back from the brick. A skip stood in the drive for a month, filling slowly with rotten timber, cracked tiles, and lengths of pipe that nobody wanted. The couple worked every weekend, and the neighbours began to nod to them in the street.

In the spring they turned to the inside. The plaster in the front room had to come down, and under it they found a fireplace that had been bricked up for decades. The chimney was swept, the hearth rebuilt, and a stack of logs appeared beside it. They painted the walls a pale grey and hung a map of the coast above the mantelpiece. Friends came to help and stayed for supper. There was talk of a vegetable patch, of chickens, of a shed at the bottom of the garden. The house, which had been silent for so long, began to fill with the ordinary noise of people living in it.

By summer the work had reached the hall, which was the last room to be finished. The floorboards were sanded and varnished, and the walls were papered in a pattern of small blue flowers. The old woman's furniture had long since gone to auction, but one thing remained: a heavy brass key that had been left on the shelf beside the stairs, too large for any lock the couple could find. They tried it in the shed, in the cupboard under the stairs, in every lock on the ground floor. It turned nothing. On a warm evening in June, while the street outside was full of the sound of someone mowing a lawn, the couple sat on the stairs and argued, without much heat, about what to do with the key. Finally the man went out to the front of the house and tried it in the lock that had never worked properly. The door swung open, and beyond it, where there had always been a brick wall, was a narrow passage leading to the garden.
